chapters.title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe

topics.title: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation

learn.hook: Imagine your whole country deciding: 'We are not the king's subjects any more, we are citizens!' That is what France did in 1789.
points: A nation-state is a state in which most citizens share a sense of common identity and history. Earlier, much of Europe was ruled by dynastic empires that held many different peoples together under one ruling family.
The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty (supreme power) from the monarch to the body of French citizens.

Revolutionaries spread the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen). The tricolour replaced the royal standard, and the Estates General, elected by active citizens, was renamed the National Assembly.

They set up a centralised administration with uniform laws for all, abolished internal customs duties, brought a uniform system of weights and measures, and made French as spoken and written in Paris the common language.

Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 (the Napoleonic Code) ended privileges based on birth, made all equal before the law and secured the right to property. But higher taxes, censorship and forced conscription made many conquered people hostile to French rule.

example.q: Think it through: Why would replacing the royal flag with a new tricolour help turn subjects into a nation?
steps: A royal flag stands for one ruling family; the people under it are only subjects.
A tricolour stood for the whole people, not for a king.
When everyone salutes the same new symbol, they feel they belong to one community with shared rights.
So symbols like the flag, new hymns and oaths built a sense of collective identity.
example.answer: The tricolour made people feel that the nation belonged to all citizens, not to the king, which strengthened a shared national identity.

learn.reallife: Our own Tiranga, the national anthem and the Republic Day parade are symbols that make crores of Indians feel they belong to one nation.

topics.title: Liberals, conservatives and the Treaty of Vienna

learn.hook: After Napoleon was defeated, Europe's kings tried to press the rewind button. But new ideas cannot be un-thought!
points: Liberalism comes from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes it meant individual freedom, equality before the law, a constitution, representative government through parliament and the safety of private property.
In revolutionary France, however, the right to vote and to be elected was given only to property-owning men. Women and men without property were left out.
In 1834 a customs union called the Zollverein was formed at the initiative of Prussia. It removed tariff barriers and cut the number of currencies in the German states from over thirty to two.

In 1815 Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria met at Vienna, hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich. The Treaty of Vienna restored the Bourbon dynasty in France and set up states on France's borders to stop future French expansion.

Conservative regimes used censorship to control newspapers and books. Revolutionaries such as Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1807, formed secret societies: Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne.

example.q: Think it through: Why did German merchants welcome the Zollverein?
steps: Before 1834 goods moving across the German states paid customs duty at many borders.
Each state also had its own currency, weights and measures, so trade was slow and costly.
The Zollverein removed tariff barriers and reduced currencies from over thirty to two.
A single economic territory made trade easier and also strengthened the wish for a united Germany.
example.answer: It removed internal tariffs and cut the number of currencies, making trade cheaper and supporting national unity.

learn.reallife: Just as one GST system replaced many separate state taxes so goods can move more easily across Indian states, the Zollverein made trade simpler across the German states.

learn.hook: Metternich once grumbled, 'When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold.' In 1830 and 1848, France sneezed loudly!
points: In July 1830 liberal revolutionaries in France overthrew the Bourbon kings and set up a constitutional monarchy headed by Louis Philippe. This sparked an uprising in Brussels, and Belgium broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
The Greek war of independence began in 1821. Supported by many West Europeans, it ended with the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832, which recognised Greece as an independent nation.

Romanticism used art, poetry, music and folk culture to create national feeling. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder said true German culture lived among the common people, das volk. In Poland, under Russian rule, using the Polish language became a sign of resistance.

The 1830s brought hardship: population grew, jobs were few and food prices rose. In 1848 food shortages and unemployment in Paris forced Louis Philippe to flee; a Republic was proclaimed and all adult males above 21 got the vote.

Also in 1848, middle-class liberals in the German states met at the Frankfurt Parliament in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848. Its 831 elected representatives offered a crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, but he rejected it. Women could only watch from the visitors' gallery.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail?
steps: It was made up mostly of middle-class professionals and lost the support of workers and artisans.
It offered the crown of a united Germany to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia.
He rejected it and joined other monarchs opposing the elected assembly.
Without royal or military support and with a narrow social base, the assembly was finally disbanded.
example.answer: It had a narrow middle-class base and was opposed by the monarchy and the army, so it was forced to disband.

learn.reallife: When the Grimm brothers collected German folk tales, they were doing something like collecting dadi-nani stories from Indian villages: saving the voice of ordinary people as part of national culture.

learn.hook: Two puzzles, two master builders: Bismarck fitted Germany together with 'blood and iron', while Cavour and Garibaldi assembled Italy piece by piece.
points: After 1848, nationalism moved away from democratic revolution. Conservatives used state power and armies to build nations.

Prussia led German unification. Its chief minister Otto von Bismarck, backed by the Prussian army and bureaucracy, fought three wars over seven years, with Austria, Denmark and France, all won by Prussia.

In January 1871 the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony at the Hall of Mirrors in Versailles. The new state focused on modernising currency, banking, and the legal and judicial systems.

In the mid-19th century Italy was divided into seven states. Only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain.

King Victor Emmanuel II and his chief minister Count Cavour led unification. Through a diplomatic alliance with France, Sardinia-Piedmont defeated Austria in 1859. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers marched into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and in 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy.

example.q: Think it through: Mazzini's uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed. Why did Sardinia-Piedmont succeed later?
steps: Mazzini relied on secret societies and revolutionary uprisings without a strong state behind them.
Sardinia-Piedmont was a kingdom with its own army and a skilled chief minister, Cavour.
Cavour made a diplomatic alliance with France, which helped defeat Austria in 1859.
Garibaldi's volunteers then won the south, and the movement came together under King Victor Emmanuel II in 1861.
example.answer: Unification succeeded when a strong state with an army and clever diplomacy took the lead, joined by popular volunteers.

learn.reallife: Just as hundreds of princely states had to be brought together into the Indian Union after 1947, Germany and Italy had to join many separate states into one country.

topics.title: War, satyagraha and the Rowlatt Act

learn.hook: A thin man in a simple dhoti returned from South Africa with an idea so powerful that an empire did not know how to fight it: the power of truth.
points: The First World War created hardship in India: defence spending rose, taxes and customs duties went up, income tax was introduced, prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, and villagers faced forced recruitment into the army.
Crop failures in 1918-19 and 1920-21 and an influenza epidemic added to the suffering; 12 to 13 million people died in the famines and the epidemic.
Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915. Satyagraha meant fighting injustice through the power of truth and non-violence, appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.

His early satyagrahas: Champaran in Bihar (1917) against the oppressive indigo plantation system, Kheda in Gujarat (1917) for relief from revenue after crop failure and plague, and the Ahmedabad cotton mill workers (1918).

The Rowlatt Act (1919) let the government detain political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi called for a nationwide satyagraha with a hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, and hundreds were killed.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the Rowlatt Act anger Indians so much?
steps: It was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council even though all Indian members opposed it.
It allowed people to be detained without trial for up to two years.
That meant the government could jail political workers without proving anything in court.
So Indians saw it as an attack on basic civil rights, and protests spread across the country.

learn.hook: Gandhiji's idea was simple: British rule stands because Indians cooperate with it. Stop cooperating, and it will wobble!
points: In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued that British rule in India survived only because of Indian cooperation. A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919, and leaders such as the brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali discussed united action with Gandhi.

At the Calcutta session (September 1920) Gandhi convinced leaders to start non-cooperation in support of Khilafat and swaraj; the programme was adopted at the Nagpur session in December 1920, and the movement began in January 1921.

The plan moved in stages: surrender of government titles, then boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods, and full civil disobedience if the government used repression.

In towns, students left government schools, teachers resigned, lawyers gave up their practice and foreign cloth was burnt. The value of imported foreign cloth fell from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore between 1921 and 1922.

In Awadh, peasants led by Baba Ramchandra protested against talukdars and landlords; the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up by October 1920. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla struggle. Plantation workers in Assam left the estates, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859. Gandhi withdrew the movement in February 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the movement in the towns slow down after a while?
steps: Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it for long.
Boycotting British institutions needed Indian alternatives such as national schools and courts.
These alternatives came up slowly, so students and teachers began going back to government schools and lawyers to courts.
Without affordable substitutes, the boycott was hard to continue.
example.answer: Khadi was costly and Indian alternative institutions were slow to come up, so many people drifted back.

learn.hook: Salt! The cheapest thing in your kitchen became the spark that lit a nationwide movement.
points: The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928 with no Indian member and was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon'. In October 1929 Viceroy Lord Irwin offered a vague 'dominion status' and a Round Table Conference.
In December 1929 the Lahore Congress, under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency, formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence), and 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Lord Irwin a letter with eleven demands, including abolition of the salt tax, with a deadline of 11 March. He then marched with 78 volunteers over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

People broke colonial laws: they made salt, picketed liquor shops, boycotted foreign cloth, refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax, and violated forest laws. Rich peasants like the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh, businessmen, industrial workers in the Nagpur region, and many women took part.

After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931, Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London in December 1931, but talks failed. Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and sought separate electorates for dalits; the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave them reserved seats, voted for by the general electorate.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the symbol of the movement?
steps: Salt is used by everyone, rich and poor, in every home.
A tax on salt therefore hurt all Indians, especially the poor.
Making salt from sea water is simple and peaceful, so anyone could break the law non-violently.
So salt united people across classes against a clearly unfair British law.
example.answer: Salt was essential for everyone, so the salt tax was seen as the most oppressive face of British rule, and breaking it united all Indians.

learn.hook: How do millions of people who speak different languages and eat different foods start feeling 'We are one'? Through songs, pictures, stories and flags!
points: Nationalism spreads when people feel they belong to one nation. This feeling grew through shared struggles and through culture: history, fiction, folklore, songs, popular prints and symbols.

The image of India as Bharat Mata was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. In the 1870s he wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland; it was later included in his novel Anandamath and was widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.

Abanindranath Tagore painted a famous image of Bharat Mata as a calm, composed and spiritual figure. Nationalists also collected folk tales and songs; in Madras, Natesa Sastri published 'The Folklore of Southern India', a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales.

During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, a tricolour of red, green and yellow was designed, with eight lotuses for the eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims. By 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag: red, green and white, with a spinning wheel in the centre.

Nationalists reinterpreted history to show India's achievements in art, architecture, science, mathematics, philosophy, crafts and trade in ancient times. They argued that colonial writers had wrongly called Indians backward.

example.q: Think it through: Why did nationalists put a spinning wheel at the centre of the Swaraj flag?
steps: The spinning wheel (charkha) stood for self-help and making our own khadi cloth.
Using khadi meant rejecting foreign, machine-made cloth.
Carrying the flag in marches showed defiance of British rule.
So the charkha turned an everyday tool into a symbol of swadeshi and self-reliance.
example.answer: The spinning wheel symbolised the Gandhian ideal of self-help and swadeshi, so the flag carried that message wherever it went.

learn.reallife: The Ashoka Chakra on today's Tiranga replaced the charkha of the Swaraj flag, but the idea of a flag that unites everyone continues.

chapters.title: The Making of a Global World

learn.hook: The aloo in your samosa and the mirchi in your chutney are travellers: they came to India from the Americas only after Columbus crossed the Atlantic, a little over five centuries ago!
points: Long before modern times, travellers, traders, priests and pilgrims carried goods, money, skills, ideas and even germs across great distances.

The silk routes, named after the Chinese silk carried along them, linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa. They existed before the Christian era and thrived almost until the 15th century. Chinese pottery and textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia travelled west, while gold and silver flowed east.
Religion and culture also moved along these routes: Buddhism, which emerged in eastern India, spread in several directions through them.

Foods such as potatoes, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes reached Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus reached the Americas. In Ireland, poor peasants depended so much on the potato that when disease destroyed the crop in 1845 to 1849, about a million people died of starvation.

By the mid-16th century the Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of the Americas was well under way. Their most powerful weapon was not guns but germs such as smallpox, to which the local people had no immunity. Silver from mines in Peru and Mexico increased Europe's wealth. Until the 18th century, China and India were among the world's richest countries.

example.q: Think it through: Why was smallpox more powerful than weapons in the conquest of the Americas?
steps: The people of the Americas had been isolated from the rest of the world for a very long time.
So they had no immunity against diseases like smallpox carried by Europeans.
The disease spread quickly and weakened whole communities, ahead of the soldiers themselves.
This made the conquest far easier than fighting alone could have done.
example.answer: Long isolation meant the local people had no immunity to diseases like smallpox, so germs weakened communities before any battle.

learn.hook: In the 1800s the world got 'connected' by three flows: goods, people and money, all moving faster than ever before.
points: Economists describe three flows in the 19th-century world economy: trade (mostly in goods like cloth and wheat), labour (people migrating for work) and capital (investment over long distances).

In Britain the Corn Laws had restricted the import of corn. When they were abolished, cheaper food flowed in from places like Eastern Europe, Russia, America and Australia; British farmers could not compete, and many people moved to cities or overseas. Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century.

Technology such as railways, steamships and the telegraph speeded up trade, and refrigerated ships allowed meat to be carried long distances. In India, the British built canal colonies in Punjab to grow wheat and cotton for export.

In 1885 European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa. In the late 1880s rinderpest, a cattle disease, spread through Africa and killed 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying livelihoods and forcing Africans into wage labour.

Indentured labourers from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and the dry districts of Tamil Nadu went to work in the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam), Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya. They created new cultures such as Hosay in Trinidad and chutney music. Indentureship was abolished in 1921.

example.q: Think it through: Why did poor Indians agree to become indentured labourers?
steps: Cottage industries were declining and land rents had risen in their home regions.
Many fell into debt and could not survive on their land.
Recruiters promised jobs abroad, sometimes giving false information about the work and living conditions.
So hardship at home pushed people to accept contracts to work in faraway plantations, mines and construction sites.
example.answer: Poverty, debt and declining home industries pushed them, while recruiters' promises pulled them to distant lands.

learn.reallife: Many people of Indian origin in Fiji, Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana are descendants of indentured labourers, and some still celebrate Diwali and sing Bhojpuri songs there.

topics.title: The inter-war economy and the Great Depression

learn.hook: One terrible war, one car factory in Detroit and one big economic crash: the years 1914 to the 1930s changed the world economy.
points: The First World War (1914 to 1918) was fought between the Allies (Britain, France and Russia, later joined by the US) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Ottoman Turkey). It was the first modern industrial war, using machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons.

Britain borrowed large sums from US banks and the US public, so the US turned from an international debtor into an international creditor. After the war, Britain faced huge debts and unemployment, and lost much of its Indian cotton market to Japan.

In the US, Henry Ford adapted the assembly line to car-making in Detroit and produced the T-Model Ford. In January 1914 he raised the daily wage of his workers to $5, roughly double the earlier wage. Mass production lowered costs, and hire purchase let people buy on credit.

The Great Depression began around 1929 and lasted till the mid-1930s. Agricultural overproduction made prices fall, and when the US cut back its overseas loans, many countries faced crisis. In the US, between 1929 and 1932 about 110,000 companies collapsed.

In India, between 1928 and 1934 exports and imports nearly halved and wheat prices fell by 50 per cent. Peasants could not pay revenue and fell into debt, and India exported precious metals, notably gold.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Indian peasants suffer badly in the Great Depression even though prices fell?
steps: Peasants sold crops in the market, so falling prices cut their incomes sharply.
But the colonial government did not reduce revenue demands.
So peasants had to pay the same tax out of much smaller earnings.
Many used up savings, mortgaged land or sold gold and silver jewellery to survive.
example.answer: Their crop prices and incomes fell, but revenue demands did not, so they fell into debt and sold land and jewellery.

learn.reallife: When people buy a phone or a scooter on EMIs today, they are using credit, much like the hire purchase that spread in 1920s America.

learn.hook: After the Second World War, world leaders met at a hotel in the small town of Bretton Woods, USA, to design new rules for money. Their plan shaped decades of growth.
points: The Second World War (1939 to 1945) was fought between the Axis powers (mainly Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US). After it, the US emerged as the dominant economic, political and military power.

Economists drew two lessons from the inter-war years: mass production can last only with mass consumption, which needs high and steady incomes and employment; and a country's economic links with the outside world must be managed carefully.

In July 1944 the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference was held at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. It set up the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with members' external surpluses and deficits, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) to finance post-war reconstruction.

The IMF and World Bank, called the Bretton Woods twins, began financial operations in 1947. Under the Bretton Woods system, exchange rates were fixed and the US dollar was anchored to gold at $35 per ounce. The US had an effective veto over key decisions.

Many newly independent developing countries, still facing poverty, joined together as the Group of 77 (G-77) to demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO), seeking real control over their natural resources, fairer prices for raw materials and better access to markets.

example.q: Think it through: Why did newly independent countries form the G-77?

So they joined together to demand a fairer New International Economic Order.
example.answer: They wanted a fairer world economic system, so they organised as the G-77 and demanded an NIEO.

learn.reallife: India is a member of the IMF and the World Bank, and news reports about World Bank loans for Indian projects like roads or clean water continue this post-war story.

learn.hook: Before big factories with chimneys, cloth for the world market was spun and woven in village cottages, with merchants running from hut to hut!
points: Proto-industrialisation was the phase before factories, when there was large-scale production for an international market that was not based in factories. It is seen in England and Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries.

Merchants moved to the countryside because in towns powerful crafts and trade guilds controlled production, regulated prices and competition, and kept new people out. Peasants and artisans in villages, short of land and income, welcomed merchants' advances to produce goods.

A merchant clothier bought wool from a wool stapler and took it to spinners; the yarn then went to weavers, fullers and dyers, and the cloth was finished in London before export. Merchants, not the workers, controlled the whole chain.

Factories grew in England from the late 18th century. Imports of raw cotton rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787. Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, and James Watt improved Newcomen's steam engine and patented his new engine in 1781; Matthew Boulton manufactured it.

Change was slow. In Victorian Britain labour was cheap and plentiful, so many industrialists preferred hand labour, especially in seasonal industries. The upper classes valued handmade goods as a sign of refinement. When James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764) came in, women who survived on hand spinning attacked the new machines.

example.q: Think it through: Why did many Victorian industrialists prefer workers to machines?
steps: Machines were costly to buy and repair, and they often broke down.
There was no shortage of poor workers willing to work for low wages.
Many industries were seasonal, so employers wanted workers only for part of the year.
Hand labour also gave the variety and fine finish that rich buyers wanted.
example.answer: Labour was cheap and plentiful, machines were costly and inflexible, and many buyers wanted handmade goods.

learn.hook: Indian cotton and silk once dressed the world. Then came Manchester's machine cloth, and later India's own mills fought back.
points: Before machine industries, Indian silk and cotton dominated the international textile market. Ports like Surat on the Gujarat coast, Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hoogly in Bengal linked India with the world. As the East India Company gained power, new ports at Bombay and Calcutta grew.

The Company appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. Weavers who took advances could not sell to other buyers, and clashes broke out in many villages in Carnatic and Bengal.

In the 19th century, British cotton goods flooded India. Indian weavers lost export markets, their local market shrank, and raw cotton became costly when the American Civil War (1860s) made Britain buy more Indian cotton.

The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854; the first jute mill in Bengal in 1855; the first spinning and weaving mill of Madras began production in 1874. Early entrepreneurs included Dwarkanath Tagore in Bengal and Parsis like Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata in Bombay. The Tata Iron and Steel works began production at Jamshedpur in 1912, and Seth Hukumchand set up the first Indian jute mill in Calcutta in 1917.

Mills hired workers through jobbers, often trusted old workers who brought people from their villages but later demanded gifts and controlled their lives. Industry grew with the Swadeshi movement's boycott of foreign cloth and during the First World War, when Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied army needs. Handloom production also survived and grew, helped by the fly shuttle.

example.q: Think it through: How did the First World War help Indian factories grow?
steps: British mills were busy producing for war needs, so exports of Manchester cloth to India fell.
Indian mills suddenly had a large home market to supply.
They also got orders for army needs: jute bags, cloth for uniforms, tents, leather boots and saddles.
Production grew so much that Manchester never fully regained its old position in India.
example.answer: Manchester imports fell and Indian mills supplied war needs, so they expanded and gained the home market.

topics.title: The first printed books: East Asia and Europe

learn.hook: Before printing, every single book was copied by hand. One Bible could take months! Then woodblocks and a clever German goldsmith changed everything.
points: The earliest print technology came from China, Japan and Korea. From about AD 594, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks. Since only one side of the thin paper could be printed, it was folded and stitched into an 'accordion book'. For a long time the imperial state was the biggest producer of printed material, such as textbooks for the civil service examination.

Buddhist missionaries from China brought hand printing to Japan around AD 768-770. The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, with six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

Marco Polo returned to Italy from China in 1295 with knowledge of woodblock printing. Paper reached Europe through the silk route. Earlier, luxury editions were handwritten on vellum, a parchment made from animal skin.

Johann Gutenberg, who grew up seeing wine and olive presses and later learnt to polish stones and make lead moulds, perfected his printing system by 1448. The first book he printed was the Bible: about 180 copies, which took three years to produce.
Between 1450 and 1550, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe. This 'print revolution' made books cheaper and created a new reading public in place of a mainly 'hearing public'.

example.q: Think it through: How did the printing press change who could read books?
steps: Hand-copying was slow and costly, so books were few and expensive.
The press could print many copies quickly, so the time and cost of each book fell sharply.
Cheaper books reached markets and many more people could buy them.
So reading spread beyond the elite, and a new reading public was born.
example.answer: It made books faster and cheaper to produce, so many more ordinary people could buy and read them.

learn.hook: India already had beautiful handwritten manuscripts on palm leaves. Then a ship to Goa brought a strange new machine: the printing press.
points: India had a rich tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and many vernacular languages, written on palm leaves or handmade paper. They were costly and fragile, so they were not widely used in everyday life.

The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani, and by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kannada languages.

Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book. By 1710, Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts, many of them translations of older works.

In 1780 James Augustus Hickey began editing the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine. He published advertisements and also gossip about the Company's senior officials. Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted him and encouraged officially approved newspapers.
The first Indian newspaper to appear was the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Warren Hastings act against Hickey?
steps: Hickey's paper published gossip about the Company's senior officials in India.
Such reports could damage the image of the colonial government.
Hastings wanted to control what was printed about British rule.
So he persecuted Hickey and encouraged newspapers that would protect the government's image.
example.answer: Hickey's paper criticised and gossiped about Company officials, so Hastings tried to silence him and backed approved papers instead.

learn.reallife: Many Indian newspapers today are more than a hundred years old. Their story began in the bustling presses of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

topics.title: Print, reform and revolution in Europe

learn.hook: One monk's list of 95 complaints, printed thousands of times, helped split the Church in Europe. Print had become powerful!
points: Not everyone welcomed print. The Latin scholar and Catholic reformer Erasmus worried that books would spread rebellious and irreligious ideas.

In 1517 the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising many practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Printed copies spread widely, leading to division in the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. Luther said, 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.'
Worried by the spread of new ideas, the Roman Church began keeping an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

By the 17th and 18th centuries literacy grew in Europe. Pedlars sold cheap chapbooks in England, and the Bibliotheque Bleue in France offered low-priced small books. Almanacs, ballads, newspapers and periodicals spread too. The writer Louise-Sebastien Mercier called the printing press 'the most powerful engine of progress'.

Many historians argue that print helped bring about the French Revolution: it popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau, created a culture of dialogue and debate, and spread literature that mocked royalty. In the 19th century Richard M. Hoe of New York perfected the power-driven cylindrical press, which could print 8,000 sheets per hour.

example.q: Think it through: Why did print help the ideas of the Reformation spread so fast?
steps: Before print, a reformer's ideas spread slowly by hand-copied letters and sermons.
Luther's Ninety Five Theses were printed in large numbers and read widely.
People could read and discuss the ideas themselves in many places at once.
So the debate spread quickly, leading to the Protestant Reformation.
example.answer: Print reproduced Luther's writings in large numbers, so many people read and debated them at the same time.

learn.reallife: Today, a post or a video can spread around India in hours. In the 16th century, the printing press did something similar for Luther's ideas.

learn.hook: In 19th-century India, presses became busy debate halls on paper, where reformers, women writers and workers all found a voice.
points: From the early 19th century, print carried lively debates on religion and society. Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821, while Hindu orthodox groups commissioned the Samachar Chandrika. In 1822 two Persian newspapers, Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar, appeared, and in the same year the Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar was published.

The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands of fatwas guiding Muslims in daily life. The first printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in 1810. Presses like the Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published religious texts in vernacular languages, so people could read them easily.

Women became readers and writers. Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote Amar Jiban, published in 1876, the first full-length autobiography in the Bengali language. In the 1880s Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai in Maharashtra wrote about the hard lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows.

Reformers wrote against caste injustice: Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri (1871); B.R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) in Madras also wrote powerfully on caste. Kashibaba, a Kanpur mill worker, wrote and published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938.

The colonial state tried to control print. After 1857, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, gave the government wide powers to censor the vernacular press. When Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote with sympathy in his paper Kesari about Punjab revolutionaries deported in 1907, he was imprisoned in 1908, sparking widespread protests.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the British pass the Vernacular Press Act in 1878?
steps: After 1857, the colonial government became suspicious of the Indian press.
Vernacular newspapers were becoming more numerous and assertively nationalist.
They criticised colonial policies in languages ordinary Indians could read.
So the Act gave the government power to censor reports and editorials and punish critical papers.
example.answer: Vernacular papers were spreading criticism of colonial rule to ordinary readers, so the government took powers to censor them.

learn.reallife: A free press that reports and debates public issues is part of Indian democracy today, protected by the freedom of speech and expression in our Constitution.
